questions.stem: Under the definition used by the United Nations, a megacity is an urban agglomeration with a population of at least:
options: 50 million
10 million
1 million
5 million
questions.explanation: The UN defines megacities as urban areas of 10 million or more people. A city of 1 million is sometimes called a million city; 5 million is the size of a large city such as Sydney.

questions.stem: A chain of large, linked metropolitan areas such as Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington, connected by transport corridors and economic flows, is best described as:
options: a primate city
an urban mega-region
a regional centre
a remote settlement
questions.explanation: An urban mega-region joins several large cities and their surrounding areas into one functional economic unit. A primate city is a single dominant city, and a regional centre serves a rural hinterland.

questions.stem: A settlement pattern in which houses and farms are spread out across the countryside, rather than grouped together, is called:
options: dispersed
nucleated
linear
clustered
questions.explanation: Dispersed settlement is typical of extensive farming areas such as the NSW wheat-sheep belt. Nucleated or clustered settlements group buildings around a centre, and linear settlements stretch along a road, river or coast.

questions.stem: Many small towns in western NSW grew in a line along a railway, with buildings stretched along the main street. This is an example of:
options: a linear settlement pattern shaped by a transport route
a dispersed settlement pattern shaped by large farms
a nucleated pattern shaped by a defensive hilltop site
a planned grid pattern shaped by a central business district
questions.explanation: Linear settlements develop along routes such as roads, railways, rivers or coastlines because access to the route is valuable. Nucleated settlements group around a central point.

questions.stem: Most of Australia's population lives in a narrow coastal strip in the east and south-east. Which pair of influences best explains this pattern?
options: tropical cyclones and monsoon floods, plus the location of the major coal deposits
reliable rainfall and a temperate climate, plus history of ports and economic development
high mountains and steep slopes along the coast, plus a lack of natural resources inland
very low rainfall and hot deserts, plus distance from markets and trade routes
questions.explanation: The south-east has a temperate climate, reliable rainfall and good soils, and colonial ports grew into the main cities and economic centres. The arid interior supports few people.

questions.stem: In an urban hierarchy, settlements are ranked according to:
options: their distance from the coast, with inland towns ranked highest
their land area, regardless of how many people live in them
their population and the range of functions and services they provide
their age, with the oldest settlements always ranked at the very top
questions.explanation: Urban hierarchies rank places by size and urban function: higher-order places such as capital cities offer specialised services, such as major hospitals and universities, that small towns do not.

questions.stem: People in villages across a region travel to a regional centre for specialist medical care, a university campus and a large shopping centre. The area from which the regional centre draws these people is its:
options: sphere of influence
urban growth boundary
central business district
ecological footprint
questions.explanation: A sphere of influence, or hinterland, is the surrounding area served by a settlement's functions. Larger, higher-order centres have larger spheres of influence.

questions.stem: In central place theory, a department store needs a much larger population to support it than a corner shop. This minimum population needed to keep a service operating is called the:
options: range
rank-size rule
primacy
threshold
questions.explanation: The threshold is the minimum number of customers needed for a service to be viable. The range is the maximum distance people will travel to use it. High-order services have high thresholds and large ranges.

questions.stem: In a country, the largest city is more than three times the size of the second-largest and dominates national economic and political life. This city is best described as:
options: a regional centre
a satellite town
a garden city
a primate city
questions.explanation: A primate city is disproportionately larger and more influential than any other city in its country, as Bangkok is in Thailand. Australia has no single primate city because Sydney and Melbourne are similar in size.

questions.stem: At the global scale, cities such as London, New York and Tokyo sit at the top of the urban hierarchy mainly because of their:
options: status as the oldest continuously occupied settlements on Earth
reliance on agriculture and mining in their surrounding regions
concentration of finance, corporate headquarters and global connections
location on the equator, which gives them a year-round growing season
questions.explanation: Global or world cities are ranked by their command functions: financial markets, corporate headquarters, media and their dense air and digital links to other cities. Their size helps, but function is what places them at the top.

questions.stem: Urbanisation refers to:
options: an increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas
an increase in the total land area covered by a single city
the movement of people from cities to rural areas and small towns
the redevelopment of run-down inner-city areas by wealthier residents
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is a rising share of people living in urban areas. Urban growth is the increase in a city's population or area, counterurbanisation is movement away from cities, and gentrification is inner-city renewal.

questions.stem: According to the United Nations' World Urbanization Prospects (2018 revision), the world's urban population first exceeded its rural population:
options: in the late 2000s
in the early 1900s
in the 1950s
in the 1970s
questions.explanation: The 2018 UN estimates put the point at which the world became more urban than rural around 2007 to 2008, using each country's own definition of urban. In 1950 only about 30% of people lived in urban areas, and the share is projected to keep rising towards 2050.

questions.stem: Most of the world's urban population growth this century is taking place in:
options: South America only
Asia and Africa
Europe and North America
Australia and New Zealand
questions.explanation: Asia and Africa are urbanising fastest and contain most of the world's growing cities, while Europe, North America and Australia are already highly urbanised and growing slowly.

questions.stem: Which combination best describes the push and pull factors driving rural-urban migration in many developing countries?
options: rural poverty and lack of land, with the attraction of urban jobs and services
urban crime and pollution, with the attraction of cheap rural housing and space
government laws forcing all young people to move to the capital at age 18
falling birth rates in cities, which create a shortage of urban schoolchildren
questions.explanation: People are pushed from rural areas by poverty, landlessness, drought and few services, and pulled to cities by jobs, education and health care. Crime and pollution are reasons some people leave cities.

questions.stem: Several small towns in western NSW have lost their bank branches, hospitals and secondary schools as populations fell. This challenge is best described as:
options: counterurbanisation, where city dwellers move into rural areas in large numbers
rural decline, where falling population reduces the threshold for services
urban sprawl, where cities spread into surrounding farmland and bushland
gentrification, where wealthier residents displace long-term residents
questions.explanation: When the population falls below the threshold needed to support a service, it closes, which encourages more people to leave. Sprawl, gentrification and counterurbanisation are processes linked to growth.

questions.stem: Which is a major environmental challenge facing large urban places such as Sydney?
options: urban heat islands, where hard surfaces make suburbs hotter than surrounding areas
desertification, where whole suburbs gradually turn into sand dunes over a few summers
permafrost thaw, where frozen ground beneath houses melts and collapses
falling sea levels, which leave harbour suburbs far from the water's edge
questions.explanation: Roads, roofs and lack of tree cover absorb and re-radiate heat, so urban areas, especially in Western Sydney, can be several degrees hotter than greener areas. The other options do not apply to Sydney.

questions.stem: Which example best shows the interdependence of rural and urban places?
options: urban and rural places compete for the same residents but share nothing else
cities buy farm produce and supply rural areas with services and finance
rural areas grow all their own food and never trade with nearby cities
cities draw all of their water from desalination plants and need no rural catchments
questions.explanation: Rural areas provide cities with food, water from catchments, energy and resources, while cities provide markets, specialist services, finance and jobs. Each depends on flows from the other.

questions.stem: Many people have moved from Sydney to coastal and inland country towns seeking a slower lifestyle and cheaper housing, often working remotely. This trend is known as:
options: urbanisation, the growing share of people living in large cities
suburbanisation, the outward spread of a city's housing estates
reurbanisation, the movement of people back into inner-city areas
counterurbanisation, sometimes called sea change or tree change
questions.explanation: Counterurbanisation is the movement of people from large cities to smaller towns and rural areas. Sea change and tree change are Australian terms for coastal and inland versions of it.

questions.stem: The Vauban district in Freiburg, Germany, is often cited as a settlement with a small ecological footprint and high wellbeing. Which features support this?
options: car-reduced streets, low-energy housing, trams and shared green space
large detached houses on big blocks served mainly by private cars
high-rise towers powered by coal with no public transport connections
gated estates surrounded by golf courses and multi-lane freeways
questions.explanation: Built on a former military base, Vauban limits car parking, uses passive and solar housing, and is linked by tram and cycle paths, giving low per-person energy use with a high quality of life.

questions.stem: Curitiba in Brazil is widely seen as a successful urban sustainability initiative because, from the 1970s, it:
options: moved its whole population into one high-rise district to protect its farmland
built a bus rapid transit network with dedicated lanes, linked to land-use planning
built a network of urban freeways so that every household could own a private car
banned all rural-urban migration so that the city's population stopped growing
questions.explanation: Curitiba combined dedicated busways, quick boarding and higher-density development along transit corridors, providing efficient, affordable transport. Its bus rapid transit model has been copied by cities around the world.

questions.stem: A council wants to make its fast-growing suburbs more sustainable. Which strategy best addresses social, economic and environmental goals together?
options: a ban on all new housing, so that the population cannot increase further
replacing parks with car parks to reduce congestion in shopping centres
medium-density housing near rail stations, with local jobs and green corridors
low-density estates on the urban fringe, served mainly by new multi-lane freeways
questions.explanation: Transit-oriented, medium-density development reduces car dependence and emissions, improves access to jobs and services and protects green space. Fringe estates increase car use and sprawl.

questions.stem: Which is the best measure of whether a sustainable housing project has improved residents' wellbeing as well as reducing environmental impact?
options: the total floor area of the development compared with nearby suburbs
surveys of residents' health and satisfaction alongside energy and water use data
the number of cars registered to residents, with no other data collected at all
the sale price of each house when it was first sold by the developer
questions.explanation: Evaluating sustainability needs indicators for both people and the environment, such as health, satisfaction and access to services, together with resource use. Price or floor area alone says little about either.

questions.stem: Mudgee, in the Central West of NSW, grew as a service centre for the surrounding farming district. Which physical factor most helped its early growth?
options: its site on a high, cold plateau, where snow attracted early tourists
its site in a desert oasis, the only water source for hundreds of kilometres
its site on the Cudgegong River valley, with water and fertile river flats
its site on a harbour, which made it the region's main seaport
questions.explanation: Mudgee lies in the Cudgegong River valley, whose water and alluvial soils supported grazing and farming, so the town grew to serve the district. It is inland, not on the coast.

questions.stem: Mudgee's economy today combines agriculture, wine and food tourism, and work at nearby coal mines. Geographically, this shows that the identity of a rural place is shaped by:
options: only its natural environment, with no influence from outside markets
government decisions alone, with no role for local businesses
its distance from the coast, which fixes its economy permanently
several physical and human processes, linking it to wider markets
questions.explanation: Rural places are shaped by both physical factors, such as climate and soils for vineyards and geology for coal, and human factors, such as tourism demand from Sydney and global coal markets.

questions.stem: Mining expansion near a rural town brings well-paid jobs, but rents rise quickly and some long-term residents and workers in tourism and retail struggle to find housing. This change is best described as:
options: a purely environmental change, with no effect on the local community
rural decline, because the town's population and services are falling
counterurbanisation, because retirees are moving from cities to the town
an economic benefit with a social cost, raising questions about equity
questions.explanation: Resource booms raise incomes and population, but housing demand pushes up rents and prices, which hurts lower-income residents. The town is growing, so this is not rural decline.

questions.stem: Mudgee and the surrounding district rely on Sydney visitors for much of their tourism trade. This is an example of a rural place's:
options: links to other places through flows of people and money
isolation from other places due to distance and remoteness
self-sufficiency, producing everything it needs locally
sphere of influence over the whole Sydney metropolitan area
questions.explanation: Tourism creates flows of visitors and spending between Sydney and the rural place, one of many links (along with markets for wine and wool and transport routes) that connect it to other places.

questions.stem: Which response would best address both the economic future and the sustainability of a rural town whose economy depends heavily on coal mining?
options: diversifying into tourism, agriculture and renewable energy while mines still operate
relying entirely on coal and approving new mines without any planning for closure
closing all local businesses so that residents must move to larger cities
banning tourism to keep housing available for mine workers only
questions.explanation: Coal demand and mine life are finite, so planning for a diverse economy before closure reduces the risk of decline. Relying on one industry leaves a town vulnerable to price falls and mine closures.

questions.stem: Parramatta, in Western Sydney, was established by the British in 1788. Which site factor made it a suitable place for an early settlement?
options: its position at the head of navigation on the Parramatta River, with fertile soils
its position on a high sandstone ridge with no reliable access to fresh water
its position on an exposed ocean beach, where ships could land cargo in heavy surf
its position in the Blue Mountains, which made it easy to defend
questions.explanation: Parramatta was where boats from Sydney Cove could travel no further upriver, and the surrounding land was more fertile than at Sydney Cove, so it became a farming settlement supplying the colony.

questions.stem: NSW planning has promoted Parramatta as the centre of the 'Central River City' in a plan for Greater Sydney as a metropolis of three cities. The main geographical aim is to:
options: replace Sydney's CBD so that the harbour city no longer has offices or jobs
bring jobs and services closer to where Western Sydney's population lives
move all of Sydney's population into the Parramatta local government area
stop all development in Western Sydney and focus growth in the eastern suburbs
questions.explanation: Many Western Sydney residents commute long distances to the eastern CBD. Growing Parramatta as a second CBD reduces travel times and spreads jobs and services more evenly across the city.

questions.stem: Large numbers of office towers and high-rise apartments have replaced older low-rise buildings in central Parramatta. This change is best described as:
options: urban renewal and densification of a major centre
rural decline caused by the loss of farm jobs
suburbanisation onto farmland at the urban fringe
counterurbanisation from Sydney to regional NSW
questions.explanation: Redeveloping existing urban land at higher density is urban renewal or consolidation. Suburbanisation spreads housing outwards at the fringe, and counterurbanisation is movement out of cities.

questions.stem: Parramatta Light Rail opened in December 2024, linking Westmead, the Parramatta CBD and Carlingford. In an investigation of Parramatta, this is best treated as:
options: evidence that Parramatta is a remote settlement with few transport links
a cause of rural decline in the farming districts west of the Blue Mountains
a strategy to reduce Parramatta's population by encouraging people to leave
a response to growth that improves transport links within the urban place
questions.explanation: Transport infrastructure is a response to population and job growth, linking homes, hospitals, the university and the CBD and reducing car dependence. It supports growth rather than reducing population.

questions.stem: A student finds that Parramatta's population has become much more culturally diverse over recent decades, with many residents born overseas. Which data source is most appropriate to measure this change?
options: a topographic map showing contour lines and spot heights around the river
rainfall records from the Bureau of Meteorology for the past twenty years
ABS census data on country of birth and language spoken at home, from several censuses
a single photograph of a busy Parramatta street taken on one weekday afternoon
questions.explanation: Comparing census data on birthplace and language across several censuses shows the nature and rate of cultural change. A single photo is unrepresentative, and maps and rainfall records measure other things.

questions.stem: Some long-term residents of an inner Sydney suburb say rising property values are forcing out lower-income households and local businesses. A geographer should treat these views as evidence of:
options: proof that urban renewal brings no benefits at all for any group living in the suburb
a physical process that is unrelated to the suburb's social and economic change
data that can be ignored because opinions are not used in geography
varying perspectives on gentrification, which benefits some groups and costs others
questions.explanation: Gentrification raises property values and attracts investment, which benefits owners and new residents, but can displace renters and long-term businesses. Investigations weigh such varying perspectives as qualitative evidence.

questions.stem: Western Sydney suburbs such as those around Parramatta and Penrith tend to have less tree canopy and record hotter summer days than suburbs near the coast. Which strategy best responds to this challenge?
options: planting street trees, cooling green spaces and using lighter roofing materials
building more multi-lane roads and large car parks to ease traffic congestion
replacing parks with paved plazas that are easier to maintain in summer
moving all new housing to the coast, where land is cheaper and plentiful
questions.explanation: Tree canopy, water features and reflective surfaces reduce urban heat, improving health and liveability. More paving increases heat, and coastal land is the most expensive in Sydney.

questions.stem: When investigating the sustainability of an urban place, why compare it with a rural place?
options: to see how processes, links and challenges differ, and how the two places depend on each other
to prove that urban places are always more sustainable than rural places
because rural and urban places always face exactly the same challenges at the same scale
because rural places have no links to cities, so comparison shows full isolation
questions.explanation: Comparing places shows how the same processes, such as population change or economic restructuring, play out differently, and highlights the flows that link them. Neither type of place is automatically more sustainable.
